item.title: Classifying K-Geodetic Graphs Via Combinatorial Designs and Distance-regularity
item.description: arXiv:2611.05762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classification of K-geodetic graphs is a fundamental problem in graph theory concerning the number of shortest paths connecting pairs of vertices. A graph is called K-geodetic if every pair of distinct vertices is joined by at most K geodesics, where a geodesic is a shortest path between two vertices. The cases K=1,2,3 correspond, respectively, to geodetic, bigeodetic, and trigeodetic graphs. Despite substantial progress in the study of their structural properties, a comprehensive classification of these graph families remains elusive. This paper develops a research framework for investigating the classification problems by combining metric graph theory, distance-regular graphs, algebraic graph theory, and combinatorial design theory. Particular attention is given to distance-regular graphs, for which the number of geodesics between vertices at a fixed distance is determined by the intersection numbers of the graph. This property converts the K-geodetic condition into a finite collection of arithmetic inequalities. We establish the resulting necessary conditions for K=1,2,3, discuss representative examples, and distinguish these conditions from the stronger requirements needed to prove the existence and classification of graphs with a given intersection array. The paper also investigates the potential role of balanced incomplete block designs (BIBDs) in constructing and organizing families of K-geodetic graphs. Finally, it proposes a computational research methodology based on constraint satisfaction, graph-isomorphism testing, exhaustive enumeration, and machine-assisted conjecture generation.
item.dc:creator: Carlos E. Frasser

item.title: How Unbalanced Must a Latin Rectangle Be?
item.description: arXiv:2611.06003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We view a $k\times n$ Latin rectangle as $n$ points in the grid $[n]^k$. Each symbol gives one point, whose coordinates are the columns it occupies. The rectangle is balanced when these points are pairwise equidistant in the $\ell_1$ metric. Its imbalance measures the distance from this ideal. We study the minimum imbalance from three sides. Constructively, we use a simulated annealing that moves symbols within rows and only penalises column clashes. Against the reference table of Voboril et al. (2025), it improves 33 of the 51 non-square values for $8\le n\le 13$, by up to 39.4%, and matches the rest. A cheap invariant, the row group, certifies that none of the 33 new rectangles is isotopic to rows of a group table, so the earlier column-swapping local search cannot reach any of them. Exactly, a computer-assisted branch and bound proves that the minimum imbalance of a $3\times 9$ rectangle is $56$. D\'iaz et al. found this value, but its optimality was open. A sharper pruning bound, derived from the identity $I=2\sum(d-t)^+$, reduces the search tree by a factor of $2.4$ to $3.3$ on the instances with $k\ge3$ that we solve. Asymptotically, the minimum imbalance is $\Theta(n^3)$ for every fixed $k$. A pigeonhole argument gives a lower constant of order $k\,4^{-k}$, and random rectangles give an upper constant of order $\sqrt k$. For $k=2$, the limit of $\min I/n^3$ exists, a permuton attains it, and it lies between $4/375$ and $0.1196$. Perfect balance is an $\ell_1$-equilateral problem, so it forces $k=\Omega(n/\log n)$ rows. For $2\times n$ rectangles, single two-minute annealing runs improve five of the seven six-hour MIP upper bounds for $14\le n\le 20$. Finally, the Lean 4 kernel checks every rectangle reported in this paper against a 74-line specification that imports only Lean's core library. We also prove the pigeonhole lower bound in Lean with Mathlib.
item.dc:creator: Zhengyu Li, Vijay Ganesh

item.title: A Polynomial Erd\H{o}s-P\'osa bound for Eulerian digraphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.06250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In [Combinatorica 1996], Reed, Robertson, Seymour and Thomas proved Younger's conjecture dating back to 1973 that states that directed cycles have the Erd\H{o}s-P\'osa property. Specifically, they showed that every directed graph $D$ contains either $k$ arc-disjoint cycles or a set of at most $f(k)$ arcs that intersect every directed cycle. The function $f$, depending only on $k$, is however notoriously large--in fact, not even elementary. The first improvement on this function was only very recently provided by Hatzel, Kreutzer, Milani, and Muzi [FOCS 2024] who showed that $f$ can be taken to be an exponential tower of height $8$. In this work, we improve this function to $O(k^4)$ in the case where the digraph is Eulerian. This also answers an open question by Wahlstr\"om [Springer Monographs in Mathematics 2018] who asked explicitly when Eulerian digraphs have a polynomial Erd\H{o}s-P\'osa property. The only other known result about Erd\H{o}s-P\'osa on Eulerian digraphs is a result from Seymour [Combinatorica 1996] who showed that $f(k)=k$ when the Eulerian digraph admits a linkless embedding in 3-space, and such an equality is not possible for general Eulerian digraphs. We also complement our positive result, by showing that the result of Seymour cannot be extended to give a linear bound ($O(k)$) on general Eulerian digraphs, by showing that even on Eulerian digraphs the lower bound for the Erd\H{o}s-P\'osa property is $\Omega(k \log k)$.
item.dc:creator: Esther Galby, Roohani Sharma, Bart van der Steenhoven

item.title: Monadically Dependent Graph Classes Have Almost Bounded Merge-Width
item.description: arXiv:2611.06804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A graph class $\mathcal{C}$ is monadically dependent if one cannot interpret all graphs in vertex-colored graphs from $\mathcal{C}$ using a fixed formula of first-order logic. We prove that every monadically dependent graph class has almost bounded merge-width, thereby confirming a conjecture of the first and the last author [STOC '25]. Our proof is algorithmic and the witnessing decompositions in the form of merge sequences can be computed in nearly-cubic time. This is a step towards the proof of fixed-parameter tractability of model checking first-order logic on monadically dependent graph classes, which is achieved in a companion paper.
item.dc:creator: Jan Dreier, Nikolas M\"ahlmann, Micha{\l} Pilipczuk, Szymon Toru\'nczyk

item.title: Boxicity of Power Graphs of Finite Nilpotent Groups
item.description: arXiv:2611.06816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The \textit{boxicity} of an undirected graph $\Gamma$, denoted as $\operatorname{box}(\Gamma)$, is the smallest non-negative integer $d$ such that $\Gamma$ can be represented as the intersection graph of axis-parallel rectangular boxes in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The \emph{power graph} of a group $G$, denoted as $\operatorname{Pow}(G)$, is an undirected graph whose vertex set is the group itself, with two elements being adjacent if one is a power of the other. We determine the exact boxicity of power graphs of finite nilpotent groups. For a cyclic group of order $n=\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i^{e_i}>1$, where the $p_i$ are distinct primes, we prove that its power graph has boxicity $\sum_{i=1}^{r}e_i-\max_i e_i$. For a finite nilpotent group $G$, let the number of noncyclic odd Sylow subgroups be denoted by $t(G)$. If $G$ has odd order or if $G$ has a cyclic Sylow $2$-subgroup, then $\operatorname{box}(\operatorname{Pow}(G))=\operatorname{box}(\operatorname{Pow}(\mathbb{Z}_{\operatorname{exp}(G)}))+t(G)$, where $\operatorname{exp}(G)$ denotes the \emph{exponent} of a group $G$. When the Sylow $2$-subgroup is noncyclic, and the odd part is nontrivial, the boxicity equals this value or one more, and we characterise precisely when each of these values is attained. The boxicity of power graphs of arbitrary finite groups and the exact boxicity of the comparability graph of the Boolean lattice were posed as open questions in Discrete Mathematics, 349(7):115017, 2026. As a consequence of our results, we answer the latter question completely and the former question partially, by computing the exact boxicity of the power graphs of nilpotent groups.
item.dc:creator: L. Sunil Chandran, Jinia Ghosh, Suraj Kumar Sahoo

item.title: Almost All 3-uniform Hypergraphs are Class 1
item.description: arXiv:2611.05622v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The chromatic index $\chi'(H)$ of a hypergraph $H$ is the smallest number of colors needed to color its edges so that no two adjacent edges share the same color. The chromatic index is trivially bounded below by the maximum degree $\Delta(H)$, and when $\chi'(H)= \Delta(H)$, we say that $H$ is Class 1. It is well known that almost every 2-graph is Class 1, and we extend this result to 3-graphs. We show for $n^{-2/3-1/200}\leq p \leq 0.99$ that the $3$-uniform binomial random hypergraph $H\sim H_{n,p}^{(3)}$ is Class 1 with high probability. We also show that this result doesn't hold for uniformities above $3$. For a broad range of $p$, when $k \geq 4$ and $k \nmid n$, the hypergraph $H \sim H_{n,p}^{(k)}$ is with high probability not Class 1.
item.dc:creator: Arnab Chaterjee, Asaf Ferber, Marcelo Sales, Mason Shurman

item.title: Sublinear Metric Distortion for Matching
item.description: arXiv:2611.05777v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study metric distortion in one-sided matching. Given $n$ agents and $n$ items in an unknown metric space, our goal is to match agents to items so that the total distance between matched pairs is small. However, instead of direct access to the distances in the metric, we are only given each agent's ranking of the items by distance. What is the smallest worst-case approximation factor (called the distortion) that a mechanism can guarantee in expectation? Despite significant interest over the last decade, the best-known guarantee has been the $O(n)$ distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship since the beginning. We give a matching mechanism with distortion $O(n^{\log_4 3})$, the first sublinear upper bound. The key idea is to use a partial matching derived from a truncated version of either Random Serial Dictatorship or the Probabilistic Serial rule. We then complete this matching using a new, general-purpose cluster completion algorithm that ensures unmatched agents receive nearby items. Along the way, we pin down the optimal distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship and Probabilistic Serial up to logarithmic and constant factors, respectively, and give improved lower bounds for truthful mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Moses Charikar, Alireza Haqi, Jabari Hastings, Yichen Huang, Prasanna Ramakrishnan

item.title: Single-Variable Connectivity in Random $k$-SAT
item.description: arXiv:2611.05981v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We resolve longstanding questions about connectivity, reconstruction,and looseness in random $k$-SAT, for sufficiently large fixed $k$ as the number $n$ of variables tends to infinity. $\textbf{Single-variable connectivity up to reconstruction.}$ At clause densities up to \[\frac{2^k}{k}\bigl(\ln k+\ln\ln k+\gamma_*-o_k(1)\bigr),\] a polynomial-time algorithm joins a typical pair of satisfying assignments with high probability, using $O_k(n)$ single-variable flips that preserve satisfiability. Here $\gamma_*\approx0.871$ arises from a refined tree-reconstruction analysis. $\textbf{Settling the reconstruction threshold.}$ Building on the tools developed for connectivity, we determine the clustering threshold defined by the reconstruction criterion to be \[\frac{2^k}{k}\bigl(\ln k+\ln\ln k+\gamma_*+o_k(1)\bigr),\] below the classical cavity prediction with constant term $1+O(\ln\ln k/\ln k)$. $\textbf{Shattering before rigidity.}$ We locate the looseness--rigidity transition at a higher density, matching the classical cavity prediction for clustering: \[\frac{2^k}{k} \left(\ln k+\ln\ln k+1+\Theta\left(\frac{\ln\ln k}{\ln k}\right)\right).\] Below the transition, we establish a stronger form of looseness: any variable of a typical solution can be reversed by logarithmically many single-variable flips that preserve satisfiability. Above it, reversing most variables of a typical solution requires changing linearly many variables (rigidity). Yet throughout an interval between reconstruction and rigidity, the solution space already splits into groups of exponentially small relative size separated by linear Hamming distance and linear energy barriers (shattering), while logarithmic looseness persists.
item.dc:creator: Chunyang Wang, Yitong Yin, Yixiao Yu, Yiyao Zhang

item.title: How many sorted projections determine n points in k dimensions?
item.description: arXiv:2611.06470v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Let $d_1,\dots,d_m$ be directions in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ge 2$. A multiset $X$ of $n$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ projects to the $m$ multisets of numbers $\{\{x\cdot d_j : x\in X\}\}$, or equivalently to the $m$ sorted lists of these numbers. How many directions are needed for these projections to determine every multiset of $n$ points? Two simple bounds are known in every dimension: more than $(k-1)\log_2 n$ directions are always needed, and $(k-1)n+1$ directions in general position always suffice. In the plane much more is known: Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron showed that almost every choice of $O(\log n \log\log n)$ directions suffices. Whether anything similar holds in higher dimensions was left open by Dym, Wellershoff, Tsoukanis, Levy and Balan. We observe that two lemmas of Hair and Sahai, proved for list recovery of random linear codes, answer that question, and by tightening their argument we show that in every dimension almost every choice of $(4k-2)\ln(2n)\ln(k\log_2 2n)+k+1$ directions suffices. For $k\le 10$ this beats the linear bound once $n$ is larger than about 100: for example, 144 directions suffice for multisets of 1000 points in the plane, and an exact computation lowers this to 133. Letting some of the random blocks in their argument fail removes a factor $\log k$: almost every choice of $O(k\log n\log\log n)$ directions suffices, uniformly in $k$ and $n$. We also show that $2k-1$ directions never determine three points, so that the logarithmic lower bound is not tight; that every $m$ directions in the plane fail on some pair of multisets of size $O(1.78^m)$, improving the bound $O(1.80^m)$ of Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron; and that for each $k$, $m$ and $n$, either almost every choice of $m$ directions works or almost none does.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Gorham Lester, Raymond Hau S{\o}rensen

item.title: Computing Forest Degree Realizations with Minimum Cardinality Domination
item.description: arXiv:2611.06482v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the Degree Realization problem with respect to a family $\mathcal{P}$ of graphs the input is a non-increasing sequence $d = (d_1,\ldots,d_n)$ of positive integers, and the goal is to decide whether there exists a simple undirected graph $G \in \mathcal{P}$, whose degrees correspond to $d$, i.e., such that $deg(G) = d$. In this paper we consider the version of Degree Realization in which the realization is required to be a forest (i.e., $\mathcal{P}$ is the family of forests). We consider \emph{optimized} Degree Realization in which the goal is to obtain a realization that minimizes an objective function $f$. That is, the goal is to find a realization $G$ that minimizes $f(G)$ among the realizations of the given input sequence. More specifically, we focus on the following functions: the size of an optimal \emph{vertex cover} and the size of an optimal \emph{dominating set}. We also consider the \emph{total} and \emph{paired} versions of both Min Vertex Cover and Min Dominating Set. We provide characterizations and linear time realization algorithms for all the above-mentioned problems. Since Min Paired Vertex Cover is closely related to Min Edge Dominating Set, our results for Degree Realization with respect to the former extend to the latter.
item.dc:creator: Amotz Bar-Noy, Omri Kosary, David Peleg, Dror Rawitz

item.title: A $2.81^n$ upper bound on the number of stable matchings
item.description: arXiv:2611.06494v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the maximum number ${\rm SM}(n)$ of stable matchings in an instance with $n$ men and $n$ women. Karlin, Oveis Gharan, and Weber (STOC 2018) proved the first single-exponential upper bound; their argument gives ${\rm SM}(n)\le 2^{17n}$ for sufficiently large $n$. Palmer and P\'alv\"olgyi (FOCS 2021) improved this bound to $3.55^n+O(1)$. We prove that ${\rm SM}(n)<2.81^n$. This brings the exponential base closer to $2.28$, the base of the best known lower bound. More precisely, we bound the number of stable matchings in each instance in terms of each person's number of stable partners, where a stable partner is someone matched to that person in at least one stable matching. Our proof assigns each person a weight determined by this number and uses these weights to bound the number of stable matchings by induction.
item.dc:creator: Ebrahim Ghorbani, Matthias Mnich

item.title: A Sub-$3^n$ Upper Bound on the Number of Stable Matchings
item.description: arXiv:2611.06604v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the problem of determining the maximum number of stable matchings. This classical counting problem was posed by Knuth and has been studied for five decades. We obtain a new $2.999^n$ upper bound on the number of stable matchings with $n$ men and $n$ women. This improves the best-known previous result by Palmer and P\'alv\"olgyi. This result gets much closer to the well-known lower bound $\frac{2.28^n}{\text{poly}(n)}$. We refine their entropy-based framework by capturing broader structural relationships among stable matchings. To capture these relationships, we introduce new frameworks, including cones and supports. This establishes the $3.332^n$ bound. We also exploit relationships among local structures and use a charging argument to improve the bound to $2.999^n$.
item.dc:creator: Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Hikaru Wada, Masataka Yoneda

item.title: Non-induced inherent graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.06636v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Concepts of avoidable paths and inherent two-rooted graphs were recently introduced for the case of induced subgraphs. In this paper, we translate this framework to the setting of not necessarily induced (NNI) subgraphs, where the structural constraints, as well as conclusions, are significantly relaxed. We develop a new sufficient condition for inherence, and use it to provide complete characterizations of inherent two-rooted paths and forks. We show that for these families, the obvious necessary condition for inherence from the induced case is sufficient in the NNI setting. To complement these results, we introduce two general methods for proving non-inherence and apply them to demonstrate the non-inherence of several classes of two-rooted trees. Keywords: subgraph, two-rooted graph, two-rooted tree, avoidable two-rooted graph, inherent two-rooted graph
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Gurvich, Matja\v{z} Krnc, Martin Milani\v{c}, Mikhail Vyalyi

item.title: On weighted partial triangulations of convex polygons
item.description: arXiv:2605.21921v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of sampling weighted partial triangulations of a convex polygon with $n+2$ sides. We consider the distribution $\pi_{n,\lambda}$ under which each partial triangulation $\sigma$ is assigned probability proportional to $\lambda^{|\sigma|}$, where $\lambda>0$ is a model parameter and $|\sigma| \in \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ denotes the number of diagonals in $\sigma$. This model belongs to a broad class of weighted geometric partition problems that include lattice triangulations and dyadic tilings, and is closely related to several classical combinatorial structures, including the full triangulations of a convex polygon and the associated Catalan structures. Our main result is a simple exact sampling algorithm for $\pi_{n,\lambda}$ with expected running time $O\big((\min\{n,n\sqrt{\lambda}\}+1)\log n\big)$, which is optimal up to the logarithmic factor.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Blanca, Alexandre Stauffer, Izabella Stuhl

item.title: Pairwise Reflection Symmetry in Frequency Rectangles
item.description: arXiv:2606.28315v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many combinatorial designs ask for equal distribution of given symbols across the entries of a matrix. The paramount examples are Latin squares, where each symbol from $\{1,\dots,n\}$ appears once per row and column of an $n\times n$ matrix. Frequency rectangles extend this to $\lambda n \times \mu n$ matrices with repeated symbols under controlled column and row frequencies. In this more general setting, we examine structural properties of pairwise reflection-symmetry, which requires that, on every pair of columns, each ordered symbol pair $(p,q)$ occurs as often as its reversal $(q,p)$. This order-balance is precisely what makes head-to-head comparisons unbiased, i.e., no symbol gains a systematic advantage from the position it occupies relative to another, a fairness demand arising for instance when scheduling tournaments or laying out comparative trials. Existence of such objects for odd $\lambda$ turns out to be remarkably more subtle than for even $\lambda$. After showing that existence holds also for sufficiently large odd $\lambda$, we initiate the search for the smallest possible value of $\lambda$ in this setting. We obtain the insight that a per-column multiplicity of $\lambda=1$ can be achieved if and only if $n$ is a power of two. We complement the existence results with a direct product construction and add several further observations on the property. Finally, we propose and evaluate a quadratically constrained integer program to computationally search for these objects. The resulting experiments reveal that many of them possess an underlying group-theoretic structure which, as we conjecture, may even be unavoidable in certain settings.
item.dc:creator: Enrico Iurlano, G\"unther R. Raidl

item.title: Graph Similarity Meets Optimal Transport
item.description: arXiv:2611.05048v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A natural way to compare two graphs is to align their vertex sets by a bijection and to measure the difference of the aligned adjacency matrices in a matrix norm. Depending on the norm, this yields, for example, the edit distance, the cut distance, the spectral distance, and the local edit distance. To make these distances applicable to graphs of different order, one can consider blowups of the graphs or, equivalently, relax bijections to fractional alignments, that is, optimal transport plans between the uniform distributions on the vertex sets, in the spirit of Gromov-Wasserstein distances. We investigate how much the optimal transport versions can differ from their bijective counterparts, that is, we quantify their integrality gaps. For the edit distance, we improve the best known upper bound on the integrality gap from 3 to 2 and the lower bound from 6/5 to 4/3. For the cut distance, we approach Lov\'asz's conjecture that $\delta_\square \le 2\delta_\square^{\rm OT}$ from both sides. We improve the previously best known upper bound $\delta_\square \le 32 \cdot (\delta_\square^{\rm OT})^{1/67}$ (Borgs, Chayes, Lov\'asz, S\'os and Vesztergombi, Adv. Math. 2008) to $\delta_\square \le C_\varepsilon \cdot (\delta_\square^{\rm OT})^{1-\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, and we construct graphs $G,H$ with $\delta_\square(G,H) = 2\delta_\square^{\rm OT}(G,H)$, establishing a factor-2 lower bound that matches Lov\'asz's conjecture. For the local edit and spectral distances, we obtain upper bounds of order $\sqrt{t\ln(1/t)}$ and $\sqrt{t}$, respectively, where $t$ is the corresponding optimal transport distance, and we show that, unlike for the edit and cut distances, no linear upper bounds are possible. Finally, we show that computing the optimal transport distances is NP-hard, and we give hardness of approximation results for the cut, spectral, and local edit distances.
item.dc:creator: Jens Breitung, Timo Gervens, Martin Grohe

item.title: Unary Functions, Automorphisms, and Unlabeled First-Order Model Counting
item.description: arXiv:2608.30580v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Every fixed first-order sentence $\varphi$ determines an enumerative sequence $n\mapsto \mathrm{FOMC}(\varphi,n)$, counting its models on the labeled domain $[n]$. We study the complexity of these sequences when logical specifications may use genuine unary function symbols and hence nested terms such as $x,f(x),f^2(x),\ldots$. We prove that, for every fixed sentence $\varphi\in \mathrm{C}^1_{=}[f]$ with one unary function and an arbitrary finite relational vocabulary, $\mathrm{FOMC}(\varphi,n)$ is computable in time polynomial in $n$. By contrast, either a second variable or a second unary function yields hardness: there is a fixed sentence in $\mathrm{FO}^2_{=}[f]$ whose model-counting function is $\#\mathrm{P}_1$-complete, and there is a fixed constant-free universal sentence in $\mathrm{FO}^1_{=}[f,g]$, using only unary predicates besides $f$ and $g$, with the same property. We also relate labeled and unlabeled enumeration exactly. For every relational sentence $\varphi$, we construct an extension $\varphi_{\mathrm{aut}}$ in which a unary function records an automorphism and $\mathrm{FOMC}(\varphi_{\mathrm{aut}},n)=n! \cdot \mathrm{UFOMC}(\varphi,n)$, where $\mathrm{UFOMC}(\varphi,n)$ counts the $n$-element models of $\varphi$ up to isomorphism. This gives a one-query exact reduction from unlabeled to labeled model counting at the same domain size. If $\varphi$ belongs to $\mathrm{FO}^k_{=}$, respectively $\mathrm{C}^k$, and its relational vocabulary has maximum arity $r$, eliminating the auxiliary function yields a single-query reduction to labeled model counting in $\mathrm{FO}^{\max\{k,r+1\}}_{=}$, respectively $\mathrm{C}^{\max\{k,r+1\}}$.
item.dc:creator: Ond\v{r}ej Ku\v{z}elka
